page_01: Some fire truck ladders reach as high as a 10-story building!
page_02: School buses are yellow so other drivers can spot them easily.
page_03: Ambulance signs are written backwards so drivers can read them in a mirror.
page_04: Garbage trucks squash the trash inside so they can carry much more.
page_05: Tow trucks use a strong hook and a winch to pull broken-down cars.
page_06: Ice cream trucks play a happy tune so everyone knows they are coming.
page_07: Monster truck tires are about as tall as a grown-up!
page_08: Race cars have wings that push them down so they grip the track.
page_09: Big rigs are called 18-wheelers because they roll on 18 wheels.
page_10: In Australia, road trains pull three or four trailers across the outback.
page_11: Car carrier trucks carry cars on two levels, like a parking garage on wheels.
page_12: Electric cars plug in to charge their batteries, just like a phone.
page_13: A camper van has a bed and a kitchen, like a tiny house on wheels.
page_14: Tractors have giant back wheels to grip soft, muddy fields.
page_15: A combine harvester cuts wheat and separates the grain in one machine.
page_16: An excavator can spin all the way around on top of its tracks.
page_17: Bulldozers push dirt, rocks and sand with a giant flat blade.
page_18: A dump truck tips its back up high to slide its whole load out.
page_19: A cement mixer's drum keeps turning so the concrete stays soft.
page_20: Tower cranes can make themselves taller, one piece at a time.
page_21: Road rollers are very heavy so they can press new roads flat.
page_22: Snowplows push snow off the road, and some spread salt to melt ice.
page_23: A bicycle uses no fuel at all, just the power of your legs!
page_24: Motorcycles lean over to the side to turn around corners.
page_25: Melbourne in Australia has one of the biggest tram networks in the world.
page_26: Steam trains burn coal to boil water, and the steam turns the wheels.
page_27: Bullet trains in Japan can zoom along at almost 200 miles per hour!
page_28: The Ghan train crosses Australia from Adelaide to Darwin, through the desert.
page_29: San Francisco's cable cars are pulled by a moving cable under the street.
page_30: Little tugboats are strong enough to push and pull giant ships.
page_31: Sailboats use the wind to move, so they need no fuel.
page_32: Submarines fill their tanks with water to sink and with air to rise.
page_33: Sydney's ferries carry people across the harbor past the Opera House.
page_34: A hovercraft rides on a cushion of air, over water and land.
page_35: Australian surf lifesavers use fast rubber boats to rescue swimmers.
page_36: The biggest container ships carry more than 20,000 metal boxes!
page_37: Old paddle steamers still carry visitors along Australia's Murray River.
page_38: Icebreaker ships have super strong fronts to crunch through sea ice.
page_39: Hot air balloons rise because hot air is lighter than cool air.
page_40: Helicopters can fly forward, backward, sideways and hover in one spot.
page_41: A jumbo jet can carry more than 400 people at once.
page_42: Australia's Flying Doctors fly planes to help sick people far from town.
page_43: Seaplanes have floats instead of wheels, so they land on water.
page_44: Gliders have no engine. They ride on rising warm air to stay up.
page_45: The Wright brothers' first airplane flight in 1903 lasted just 12 seconds.
page_46: Water bomber planes scoop up water from lakes to put out fires.
page_47: Blimps float because they are filled with helium, a gas lighter than air.
page_48: A rocket must fly over 17,000 miles per hour to circle the Earth!
page_49: The space shuttle blasted off like a rocket and landed like a plane.
page_50: Astronauts first drove a Moon buggy on the Moon in 1971.
